draft.title: Entwurf eines Dritten Gesetzes zur Änderung des Brennstoffemissionshandelsgesetzes
draft.version: BT 21/7869, dated 7 September 2026; current archived parliamentary PDF.
draft.relevant_provision: The proposed 2027 carbon-price corridor; the narrow research-description correction does not depend on draft wording.
draft.version_limit: Committee cover refers to the 7 October hearing. Authored date is 5 October; actual delivery not independently authenticated.

history.event: Identified in systematic factual-check inventory; narrow staged record awaits explicit independent context and source review.

verification.scope: A narrow description of cited evidence; no finding of intent or general adjudication of energy policy.

card.law_is_about: Extending national fuel-carbon pricing through the transition to the European system.
card.they_want: Abolish the national fuel-emissions trading law.
card.they_claim: The cited wind-farm infrasound levels are already around the hearing or perception threshold.
card.the_problem: The reported spatial levels concern around 1 Hz. The cited agency guidance requires frequency-specific comparison and does not establish a 96–101 dB perception threshold at that frequency.

claim_quote.original: Das liegt dann bereits an der Hör-/Wahrnehmungsschwelle
claim_quote.translation_en: That is then already at the hearing/perception threshold

locator.paragraph: Immediately after the 90–95 dB at 1 km and+6 dB at 500 m comparison

counter_quote.original: Dabei muss der Pegel umso höher sein, je tiefer die Frequenz ist.
counter_quote.translation_en: The lower the frequency, the higher the level must be.

correction: Compare sound levels at the same frequency and with the same acoustic measure. Mattsson’s cited maps describe a 1 Hz third-octave band. The LfU guidance gives about 103 dB for perception at 8 Hz, and says perception below 2 Hz had not been described and would require extremely high levels. It does not establish that the stated roughly 96–101 dB levels near 1 Hz meet the hearing/perception threshold. Its greater-than 120 dB military-aircraft analogy is not a measured universal 1 Hz threshold.
effect: Qualifies the claimed perception-based basis for the wind-health comparison supporting abolition. It does not disprove the paper’s reported sound levels, researchers’ symptom reports or every possible non-auditory effect.
limits: Hearing/perception and health harm are different propositions. Individual sensitivity and non-auditory effects remain uncertain; levels below a typical hearing threshold are not thereby shown harmless. The cited guidance discusses substantial individual variation near 20 Hz, which cannot simply be transferred quantitatively to 1 Hz. The distance maps combine measurements and modelling; no separate factual-error finding is staged from ambiguous measured-versus-modelled wording.
context_and_alternatives: The entire infrasound passage and source sections were read, including the anecdotal symptoms and the simulated spatial maps.
The statement’s first numerical sentence names no frequency, but the cited source’s relevant maps and the closing anecdote concern around 1 Hz. The frequency-specific scope must remain explicit.
The agency guidance’s illustrative hearing-sound comparison is explicitly not a physically interchangeable comparison and supplies no exact universal threshold below 2 Hz.
The general claim that wind turbines harm health more than climate change remains broader and unestablished; this record only addresses the threshold inference.
materiality_explanation: Minor: the cited frequency-specific evidence does not support the asserted threshold comparison. The correction is confined to that supporting technical premise and does not establish an overall health benefit or harm.
direction_explanation: True narrowly: an asserted perceptibility threshold strengthens the author’s wind-harm premise supporting abolition; correcting the comparison narrows that support.

confidence.text_source_mismatch: High for the cited frequency-specific guidance; individual responses and broader health effects remain uncertain.
